steps.say: The modern diagnosis is built on scans and blood tests, because examination alone is missing too many cases. Diagnosis now rests on blood tests plus ultrasound or computed tomography rather than history and examination alone. Magnetic resonance imaging is being added at some centres to cut radiation in children.
steps.tx: Diagnosis now rests on blood tests plus **ultrasound** (first line scan) or **computed tomography** (CT for unclear cases) rather than history and examination alone, with **magnetic resonance imaging** (MRI avoiding radiation) added at some centres to cut radiation in children.

vis.alt: Abdominal diagram showing periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain migration with McBurney point, Rovsing, psoas and obturator signs.
vis.caption: Scans and blood tests now anchor diagnosis, with MRI cutting radiation at some centres. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Care pathways are standardising every step from antibiotics to discharge, and keyhole surgery leads the way. Clinical pathways are standardising antibiotics, technique and near zero outpatient opioids across the unit. Laparoscopic appendectomy remains the standard operation for most children.
steps.tx: **Clinical pathway** (agreed care bundle) standardises **antibiotics** (timed doses), technique and near zero outpatient opioids, and **laparoscopic appendectomy** (keyhole removal) is the standard operation with faster recovery and fewer wound infections than open surgery. Nurses, anaesthetists and surgeons follow the same written bundle daily.

vis.alt: Four panel examination guide showing McBurney migratory pain, Rovsing sign, psoas stretch and obturator rotation tests.
vis.caption: Standardised pathways pair careful examination with keyhole surgery as the standard operation. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Simple cases need one well chosen antibiotic and a timely but unhurried operation. Simple appendicitis gets preoperative piperacillin tazobactam monotherapy covering gut flora. Timing of surgery is safe within 24 hours without added perforation risk, so night operations are becoming rare.
steps.tx: **Simple appendicitis** (unruptured inflamed appendix) gets preoperative **piperacillin tazobactam** (broad gut cover) monotherapy, and **timing of surgery** (operating within a day) is safe within **24** hours without added perforation risk, allowing daylight operating. Allergy history is checked before the first dose is administered.

steps.say: Ruptured disease with pus or mass follows a different road, often without an immediate operation. Complicated appendicitis continues antibiotics after surgery or uses percutaneous drainage with or without delayed interval appendectomy. The choice is resting on the size of the collection and the state of the child.
steps.tx: **Complicated appendicitis** (rupture with pus or mass) continues antibiotics after surgery or uses **percutaneous drainage** (needle drain by radiology) with or without delayed **interval appendectomy** (later planned removal) once the child stabilises and inflammation settles. Small collections often settle with antibiotics alone.

steps.say: Perforation raises the stakes because abscess follows so often, and drains are saving many reoperations. Up to 40 percent of perforated cases develop postoperative abscess needing drainage or continued antibiotics. Watch fever, pain and inflammatory markers after every ruptured case.
steps.tx: Up to **40** percent of perforated cases develop **postoperative abscess** (walled pus after surgery) needing **drainage** (needle or surgical emptying) or continued antibiotics. Fever with **perforation** (ruptured wall) history mandates imaging before discharge planning. Ultrasound guided drainage succeeds in most collected cases.

nodes.label: Fever or pain suggests abscess in up to 40 percent
Image then drain or prolong antibiotics

steps.say: Carefully chosen children are avoiding the operation altogether, though questions remain open. A multi institutional clinical trial found nonoperative management acceptable for carefully selected uncomplicated appendicitis. Long term efficacy needs more study before this becomes routine for every child.
steps.tx: A multi institutional **clinical trial** (hospital group study) found **nonoperative management** (antibiotics without surgery) acceptable for carefully selected **uncomplicated appendicitis** (simple inflamed appendix), though long term efficacy needs more study before routine adoption. Recurrence after antibiotics alone reaches a third within a year.

steps.say: The pandemic is teaching surgeons to weigh the anaesthetic as heavily as the appendix. Nonoperative care proved useful during COVID-19 in children whose concurrent respiratory infection made anesthesia hazardous. Avoiding intubation during active infection is protecting both child and team.
steps.tx: Nonoperative care proved useful during **COVID-19** (pandemic coronavirus) in children whose concurrent **respiratory infection** (active chest infection) made **anesthesia risk** (airway danger under anaesthetic) hazardous, favouring antibiotics until the chest clears. Shielded lists with tested staff kept urgent surgery running safely throughout.

steps.say: A walled off collection is drained first and removed later, once the storm has passed. Contained abscess in complicated appendicitis is drained percutaneously first, with delayed interval appendectomy weeks later once inflammation settles. The appendix is coming out through calm tissue at the second sitting.
steps.tx: **Contained abscess** (walled pus collection) is drained percutaneously first, with delayed **interval appendectomy** (planned later removal) weeks later once **inflammation** (tissue swelling and anger) settles and planes are safe for surgery. The appendix usually lifts out easily through calm, non friable tissue.
